statement: For how many integers $n$ with $1 \le n \le 100$ is $\dfrac{n}{120}$ a terminating decimal but $\dfrac{n}{36}$ not a terminating decimal?

choices.misconception: I mixed up the two conditions and counted the multiples of 9, which are the $n$ that make $n/36$ terminate.
I counted the 33 multiples of 3, which make $n/120$ terminate, and forgot to remove those that also make $n/36$ terminate.
I thought $n/120$ terminates when 3 does not divide $n$, and every such $n$ fails for 36, so I counted the 67 non-multiples of 3.
I counted the 89 values that are not multiples of 9, which handles $n/36$, and ignored the condition on $n/120$.

hints: A fraction in lowest terms terminates exactly when its denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5.
Factor $120$ and $36$. For each fraction, decide which factors $n$ must cancel so that only 2s and 5s remain.
$n/120$ terminates exactly when $3 \mid n$, and $n/36$ terminates exactly when $9 \mid n$. Count multiples of 3 that are not multiples of 9.

solutions.reliable: Since $120 = 2^3 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$, the fraction $n/120$ terminates exactly when $n$ cancels the single factor of 3, that is, when $3 \mid n$. Since $36 = 2^2 \cdot 3^2$, the fraction $n/36$ terminates exactly when $9 \mid n$. So we want multiples of 3 that are not multiples of 9. Between 1 and 100 there are $\lfloor 100/3 \rfloor = 33$ multiples of 3 and $\lfloor 100/9 \rfloor = 11$ multiples of 9, all of which are multiples of 3. The answer is $33 - 11 = 22$. Transferable idea: whether a fraction terminates depends only on the primes other than 2 and 5 left in its reduced denominator.
